title: Dual-Task Capacity Laboratory
scopeNote: This keeps the performed blocks and the enforced order that makes a cost measurable: each task alone first, then both. The difficulty manipulation, the response-overlap manipulation that separates a bottleneck at the response from one earlier, and the block-by-block record stay in the longer version. The block order is fixed rather than counterbalanced, which is a real limitation the caution states.
summary: Two trivial speeded tasks are performed alone and then together. Both slow down, and the cost for each is measured against the learner's own single-task speed rather than against anyone else's.
learningObjectives: Explain why a dual-task cost can only be measured against a single-task baseline.
Recognise that two easy tasks interfere even when neither is difficult.
Recognise that the cost is usually shared unequally between the two tasks.
Explain why the interesting question is what doing two things costs rather than whether it is possible.
Identify fixed block order and browser timing as limits on what a classroom block shows.
interactionTypes: three performed blocks in an enforced order
two distinct judgements with two distinct response mappings
a dual block where both stimuli appear at once and both must be answered
a paired bar chart of each task alone and together
a table of both costs and dual-block accuracy
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted. Every reaction time is measured and analysed in the browser and is gone when the page is closed.
accessibilityNotes: Four arrow keys or four labelled buttons, each naming the key it duplicates, and no trial is ever timed out. Only the keypads a block actually needs are shown, and keys are disabled until a stimulus is present so an accidental press cannot be recorded. On a dual trial answering one task disables that keypad and leaves the other live, so the state of the trial is visible rather than remembered. The display carries a description naming what is showing, so a trial can be answered without seeing the panel. The chart distinguishes alone from together by fill against outline as well as by position, and carries a description giving all four means and both costs; the table repeats them. Where cleaning leaves too few usable trials the chart and table are hidden rather than drawn empty. Nothing fades, moves or animates.
dataStatus: The learner's own reaction times, produced in the moment. Nothing is a norm and nothing is compared with anyone else.
simulationNotes: Sixteen trials of each task alone and twenty with both together, in a fixed order. The two tasks use different judgements, one on identity and one on position, and different response keys, so a dual trial requires two distinct actions rather than one repeated. On a dual trial both stimuli appear together and both must be answered, in whichever order the learner chooses; which task they protect is part of what the result shows, and both costs are reported rather than one combined figure. Responses under 150 ms or over 4 seconds are counted, reported and kept out of the means, as are errors. The fixed block order means any practice effect across the session is mixed into the dual-task cost and would make it look smaller than it is; counterbalancing across people is what a proper design would do, and the caution says so.
readmeTopic: what doing two easy things at once actually costs, measured against your own baseline
